turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in. I'm Dr. Ellison. Have a seat wherever is comfortable.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate you fitting me in. I am here about my right knee, if that is all right.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Of course. How long has it been bothering you?

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): I nearly said three weeks, but that is not accurate. It started after I knelt on the patio doing yard work, and that was six weeks ago. It is a dull ache on the inner side of the right knee, and rest does ease it.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Six weeks. Any twist, pop, or fall?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing dramatic. I simply stayed on my knees too long, which was foolish.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Inner side of the right, just to be sure I have it?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. The right knee, inner side. Not the left.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): And stairs?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Going down stairs is distinctly worse than going up. I take them one at a time now.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does the knee lock, or give way under you?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No. It has never given way, and it does not lock.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any swelling you have noticed?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. I would not want to commit to saying it swells.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Morning stiffness?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. Perhaps twenty minutes, and then it loosens once I have been walking.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have you tried anything for it?

[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Ibuprofen. I almost told you seventy-five milligrams, but that is the wrong medicine entirely. They are four hundred milligram tablets, and I take one by mouth with food, about three evenings a week, when the ache is bad.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not every day, then?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): That is correct. Not daily.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any heartburn or stomach pain from those?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No, none at all.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Chest pain? Shortness of breath? Dizziness?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No, Doctor. I have had none of those.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Headaches?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. I would not call them headaches, to be precise.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fair enough, I'll leave that one. Let me examine the knee.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Please do. I washed up before I came, though the waiting room was rather warm.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not warm to touch, no redness, and you bend it fully. There is tenderness right on the inner joint line.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, that is the spot. It is tender if I press it myself as well.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm thinking this is a strain along the inner knee. I don't see a reason for an x-ray today.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): That is reassuring. I did bring a form for the community center walking group. The young woman at the desk already dated it. We can leave it until the end if you prefer.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll sign it before you go. Walking on level ground should be fine. There is something else, though. The nurse flagged your blood pressure.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah. She did say it was high. I believe I have white coat hypertension. Offices make me tense, I'm afraid.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me read her numbers out loud so we both hear them. She recorded one sixty-eight over ninety-six.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): That does sound high. I had a cup of coffee while I waited, which may not have been wise. The magazines out there are rather bleak, if I may say so.

[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Coffee can lift it a few points. I'm going to repeat it with your arm relaxed and your feet on the floor. First look I thought one sixty-four over ninety-two. No, the column settled at one fifty-two over eighty-eight.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Still higher than I care for, I'm afraid.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pulse is eighty-eight... no, I rushed the count. It is seventy-six and regular.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): My father had a stroke at seventy-two. I mention it only in passing. He smoked heavily. I never have.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): I appreciate you saying so. A stroke in your father is worth having on the record. And you yourself have never smoked?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Never. Not a single cigarette.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are you on any blood pressure medicine now?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I have never been given one.

[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me think this through out loud. The nurse's reading was one sixty-eight over ninety-six, and mine is one fifty-two over eighty-eight, so both are up. It may be white coat, and I cannot honestly call it that from two office readings alone. I am not starting a tablet today.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): I am glad of that. I would prefer to avoid a daily medicine if it is not necessary.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): What we will do is home monitoring. Use an upper-arm cuff, not a wrist one, seated, morning and evening, for seven days. Write every reading down.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): My wife has an upper-arm cuff from her own physician. It is a year or two old, I believe. Will that serve?

[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes, if it still fits the upper arm. If the home average stays under one thirty-five over eighty-five, we leave medicine alone. If it does not, we discuss a tablet at the follow-up. Not before.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): That seems entirely reasonable.

[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back in two weeks with the log. If a home reading is over one eighty on top, or you get chest pain or real shortness of breath, don't wait for me. Call the office or go to urgent care.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): I understand. And for the knee, may I continue the ibuprofen as I have been?

[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes. One four hundred milligram tablet by mouth with food, up to three evenings a week, ice the knee fifteen minutes after you have been on it, and try not to kneel. I'll sign that walking form on your way out. Flat walking is fine.

spec.situation: Patient attends for something minor (a knee or a form) and the nurse finds high BP; BP read aloud twice with different numbers; patient says it is white coat; family history of stroke said in passing; no tablets started today, home monitoring arranged.
features: ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.
self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.

Doctor advised to use a seated position with arm relaxed and feet on the floor for blood pressure measurement.
If home blood pressure average stays under 135/85, medicine will be left alone.
Red-flag advice included 'real' shortness of breath, not just any shortness of breath.
